proposals.impact: closes 29-point open-rate gap between Money Worship (37.5%) and Money Vigilance (66.67%)
proposals.observation: The Money Worship automation has a 37.5% open rate across 16 sends. Money Vigilance sits at 66.67% across 12 sends, and Money Avoidance at 52.63% across 19 sends. Money Worship is the weakest by 15 to 29 points. Subject line is the only variable that determines whether an email gets opened, and it is the smallest single-file change available. The Money Worship script tends toward aspiration framing ("earn more, deserve more") which ICP 25-35 self-development earners read as either out of reach or vaguely performative. A subject line that names a specific, uncomfortable money thought will outperform a motivational one with this audience.
proposals.proposal: Replace the current Money Worship email-1 subject line with one that meets the ICP where their actual quiet anxiety lives, rather than where they wish they lived. The new line names a real cognitive pattern (tying self-worth to a salary number) without any banned spiritual or hustle framing. It passes the Sultanic test because it refers to a specific feeling this segment reports, not a generic motivational prompt.

proposals.new_text:
---
title: "The bank tab you've had open for three days without clicking it"
pubDate: 2026-07-21
description: "Leaving the tab open feels like almost looking. Here is what that almost costs."
tags: ["money avoidance", "behavioural money"]
---

Most people I work with are not ignoring their money because they are lazy. They open the tab. They just do not click through to the balance. The tab stays open for days as a kind of proof to themselves that they are *about to* deal with it.

I did the same thing for longer than I want to admit. The tab sat there. My gym bag sat by the door. I told myself I was one tidy Sunday away from getting on top of it.

The cost is not just the interest on the credit card or the ISA contribution that didn't go in. The cost is the low-level hum of dread that runs underneath a day when you know there is a number you have not faced. That hum is exhausting in a way that is hard to name to someone who has never felt it.

The tab is not the problem. The tab is the signal that something underneath feels too large to look at directly.

If you want to understand what is actually driving the avoidance, the [money psychology quiz](/quiz) takes four minutes and tells you something more precise than "you need to budget better."

Joel Watts, MSc Behavioural Economics | Qualified Financial Planner
